sourceNote: Mineral identity and Mohs hardness are facts. 'modernAssociations' are modern crystal-practice beliefs with no demonstrated physical effects, and they are labelled as such in the UI. In this game, stones are used as tactile grounding anchors: weight, temperature and texture. Ethical sourcing varies widely; second-hand or known-origin stones are better. 'history' is the documented history of the stone or its name (Pliny the Elder's Natural History; Theophrastus; GIA and American Gem Society history pages; Whitby Museum and the V&A on jet; the Met and published reviews on Egyptian malachite eye paint; Inuktitut Magazine 125 for the labradorite story), with legends marked as legends. 'charmMeaning' is the short modern-practice meaning shown in a charm bag: a belief, not an effect.

crystals.name: Hematite
crystals.tactile: Surprisingly heavy for its size, cool to the touch, and glassy smooth. A very good stone for 'feel the weight in your palm'.
safetyNotes: Strongly magnetic 'hematite' jewellery is usually a synthetic called hematine. Keep it away from pacemakers and bank cards.
crystals.history: Named from the Greek haima, blood, for the red streak it leaves when scratched (Theophrastus; Pliny's haematites). Red ochre, coloured by hematite, is one of the oldest pigments people used.

crystals.name: Smoky quartz
crystals.tactile: Cool, hard and glassy. Translucent browns and greys, like looking through woodsmoke.
careNotes: Much commercial smoky quartz is artificially irradiated clear quartz.
crystals.history: In Scotland it's 'cairngorm', after the mountains where it was found: from the 1700s it was set in Highland plaid brooches and the pommel of the sgian-dubh.

crystals.name: Clear quartz
crystals.tactile: Hard, cold at first, and slowly warming in your hand. Rainbows appear where it's fractured inside.
careNotes: Can focus sunlight like a lens. Don't leave it in a sunny window near fabric.
crystals.charmMeaning: for clarity, and a clean start
crystals.history: Greek krystallos, ice. Pliny the Elder believed rock crystal was ice frozen so hard it could never melt, since it was found near Alpine snows.

crystals.name: Amethyst
crystals.mineral: Quartz (SiO₂), purple from iron and natural irradiation
crystals.tactile: Faceted points with sharp-ish edges, or smooth when tumbled. Purple deepens toward the tips.
crystals.charmMeaning: for a clear head, and sobriety
crystals.history: Greek amethystos, 'not drunk': Pliny records the old belief that it kept the wearer sober. The Dionysus myth about it was written much later, by the French poet Remy Belleau in the 1500s.

crystals.name: Rose quartz
crystals.tactile: Milky, soft pink, and usually tumbled very smooth. Pleasant to rub with your thumb.
crystals.charmMeaning: for love, and being kind to yourself
crystals.history: Carved into beads and seals in the ancient Near East and the Roman world; its link to love and to Venus is modern crystal lore built on that.

crystals.name: Black tourmaline (schorl)
crystals.tactile: Long, striated ridges run along its length, so you can feel the grooves under your fingernail.
careNotes: Brittle across its length. Raw pieces can splinter.
crystals.charmMeaning: for protection, and keeping things out
crystals.history: It builds an electric charge when warmed or rubbed, so it picks up dust and ash; that property was studied by 18th-century scientists. (The often-told Dutch name 'aschentrekker', ash-puller, couldn't be confirmed.)

crystals.name: Moonstone
crystals.tactile: Smooth and pearly, with a bluish glow (adularescence) that floats across the surface as you tilt it.
careNotes: Has cleavage planes, so it can crack if knocked.
crystals.charmMeaning: for the moon, dreams and new beginnings
crystals.history: Romans thought it was made of moonlight and tied it to the moon goddess; in India it's 'moon's light' and a traditional wedding gift. Art Nouveau jewellers (Lalique, Tiffany) loved it.

crystals.name: Labradorite
crystals.tactile: Dull grey until it catches the light just right, then flashes of blue, green and gold appear. Good for an 'I'll notice when it changes' focus exercise.
crystals.history: Named for the Labrador coast, where Moravian missionaries saw it among Inuit people around 1770. An Inuit story recorded in Inuktitut Magazine tells of northern lights trapped in the rock, and a hunter's harpoon that freed most of them.

crystals.name: Carnelian
crystals.tactile: Waxy and warm-looking, in translucent orange-red. It glows like an ember against light.
careNotes: Much commercial carnelian is heat-treated or dyed agate.
crystals.history: The most common gemstone of ancient Egypt, tied to the sun and to blood and life: heart amulets and Eye of Horus amulets were carved from it.

crystals.name: Obsidian
crystals.tactile: Glass-smooth and black, with a mirror-like shine when polished.
safetyNotes: Broken or raw obsidian has edges sharper than a scalpel. Only handle tumbled pieces.
crystals.history: Volcanic glass, knapped into blades for thousands of years and polished into mirrors in Mesoamerica.

crystals.name: Selenite
crystals.tactile: Silky, fibrous and soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Feels faintly warm compared with quartz.
careNotes: Water damages it: it dissolves and pits. Never wash or soak it.
Most stones sold as 'selenite' are the fibrous variety, satin spar.
crystals.history: Named for Selene, the Greek moon. Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, and it dissolves in water.

crystals.name: Malachite
crystals.tactile: Banded swirls of deep and light green, like rings in a cut tree. Polished pieces are cool and silky.
careNotes: Soft, so it scratches easily. Keep away from acids and household cleaners.
safetyNotes: Dust from cutting or sanding is toxic. Never make 'gem elixirs' or put it in drinks. Wash your hands after handling raw pieces.
crystals.history: Ground into green eye paint (udju) in ancient Egypt from about 4000 BCE; its Sinai mines were linked to the goddess Hathor.

crystals.name: Tiger's eye
crystals.tactile: Golden-brown bands shimmer and roll as you turn it (chatoyancy), like light on water.
safetyNotes: Polished stones are safe to handle, but they should never be cut or ground at home, because the original fibres were a form of asbestos.
crystals.history: Its moving band of light (chatoyancy) comes from fibres inside the quartz; that 'eye' made it a watchful stone in modern lore.

crystals.name: Jet
crystals.mineral: Lignite: fossilised wood (not a mineral crystal)
crystals.tactile: Very light for a black stone, and warm almost at once in your hand. Velvety where it's polished.
careNotes: Soft: keep it away from harder stones, which scratch it.
safetyNotes: Black glass is often sold as jet: real jet feels warm and light.
crystals.history: Fossilised wood. After Prince Albert died in 1861, Queen Victoria wore Whitby jet for the rest of her life, and jet became the stone of mourning across Britain.

crystals.name: Amber
crystals.tactile: Light, and warm in the hand straight away. Rub it on wool and it smells faintly of pine.
careNotes: Soft and easily scratched; keep it from heat and perfume.
safetyNotes: Plastic and copal are often sold as amber.
Amber teething necklaces are a choking and strangulation risk: never for babies.
crystals.history: Fossil tree resin, washed up on Baltic shores after storms. In Lithuanian legend it's the pieces of the sea goddess Jūratė's amber palace, or her tears. The Greeks said it was the tears of the sun's daughters.

crystals.name: Mira's stone
crystals.mineral: A garden pebble with a ring of white quartz (or calcite) all the way around: a vein that filled a crack in the rock
crystals.tactile: Grey, flat and smooth as soap. Your thumb finds the white line without looking.
careNotes: Nothing. It's been in your pocket for years.
crystals.history: From Mira's garden. In British and wider European coastal folklore, a stone with one unbroken white ring all the way around is a wishing stone: trace the line with a finger, make a wish, and give it back to the sea, or give it to someone else. Mira gave it to you.
crystals.charmMeaning: for being held, and a wish (a wishing stone)
